findings.quote: useless against viruses and dangerous only in true penicillin allergy
findings.explanation: An absolute safety claim that the page itself contradicts: sideEffects, warnings and cautions list C. difficile colitis, the very common rash in glandular fever (drug avoided), cholestatic liver injury with co-amoxiclav, seizures at high doses in kidney failure, crystalluria and a warfarin interaction. 'Only' makes the summary read as a promise of safety outside allergy.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop 'dangerous only in true penicillin allergy'. For example: '...; it has no effect on viruses and is not used in people with a history of true penicillin allergy.'

findings.quote: A non-drowsy second-generation antihistamine that blocks histamine H1 receptors to relieve hay fever, hives and other allergic symptoms. It works within about an hour, is taken once a day and is sold without prescription, but it is the most sedating of the modern antihistamines
findings.explanation: The same sentence calls cetirizine 'non-drowsy' and 'the most sedating of the modern antihistamines'. sideEffects.common says sleepiness is its most common effect and the cautions advise avoiding driving when drowsy. 'Non-drowsy' is wrong for this drug and could lead a reader to drive or use machinery unprepared (UK wording is 'non-sedating' or 'less sedating', and drowsiness is still listed for cetirizine).
findings.suggestedFix: Write 'a second-generation (less sedating) antihistamine' and keep the statement that it is the most likely of the modern antihistamines to cause drowsiness.

findings.quote: which is why doses are capped in kidney impairment, in people of Asian ancestry and with ciclosporin or some HIV medicines
findings.explanation: Says doses are 'capped' with ciclosporin, but cautions[0] ('Ciclosporin: do not combine') and the contraindications block (absolute; about sevenfold rise in exposure) say the combination is contraindicated, as the UK SmPC does. Capping rosuvastatin at 5 mg with ciclosporin is US labelling. A reader could conclude the combination is allowed at a lower dose in the UK.
findings.suggestedFix: '...doses are capped in kidney impairment, in people of Asian ancestry and with some HIV medicines or gemfibrozil; ciclosporin is contraindicated.'

findings.quote: Increased suicidal thoughts in the first weeks, particularly under 25: close follow-up
findings.explanation: Red-flag effect with no action for the reader: 'close follow-up' is a clinician-side statement and nothing on the page tells a reader what to do about new or worsening suicidal thoughts. Other serious effects (serotonin syndrome on this page) and the prednisolone page ('report to a doctor or NHS 111') do give an action. A UK-first page should signpost urgent help.
findings.suggestedFix: Add that new or worsening thoughts of suicide or self-harm, or marked agitation or distress, after starting or changing the dose need urgent contact with a GP or NHS 111, and 999 or A&E if in immediate danger (Samaritans 116 123 is a free 24-hour listening service); young people under 25 and their carers are told to watch for this in the first weeks.

findings.quote: Stopping suddenly after long use carries a high risk that gout will return or worsen, so a doctor reduces the dose slowly if it has to be withdrawn
findings.explanation: No withdrawal taper is recognised for allopurinol: after stopping, serum urate climbs back over days to weeks and gout attacks recur over months; there is no abrupt rebound. 'A doctor reduces the dose slowly' is not in the NHS or MedlinePlus pages cited and conflicts with the advice elsewhere on this page to stop at once and seek help for a rash (possible serious hypersensitivity reaction), which a reader could take as a reason to delay stopping.
findings.suggestedFix: 'Stopping allopurinol lets uric acid rise again and gout attacks may return, so it is not stopped without talking to the prescriber, except that a rash or other signs of a serious reaction need urgent medical advice.'

findings.quote: NICE: an alternative first-choice for low-severity community-acquired pneumonia in penicillin allergy, and added to amoxicillin (or used as an alternative) for moderate severity
findings.explanation: To my knowledge NICE NG138 recommends amoxicillin, with doxycycline or clarithromycin (erythromycin in pregnancy) as the alternatives or add-on for atypical cover; azithromycin is not one of its named agents, so the note attributes to NICE a recommendation the guideline does not make. The amoxicillin page in this slice states the NICE position correctly ('atypical pneumonia doxycycline or clarithromycin'), so the two pages disagree. usedFor[0] ('particularly in penicillin allergy') inherits the same problem.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the NICE attribution, or say that azithromycin is licensed for mild to moderately severe community-acquired pneumonia while NICE NG138 names doxycycline or clarithromycin (erythromycin in pregnancy). Reword usedFor[0] to match.

findings.quote: Chlamydia and some other sexually transmitted infections (single dose)
findings.explanation: In current UK guidance (BASHH 2018, NICE CKS) doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days is first-line for uncomplicated genital chlamydia; azithromycin is the alternative (now 1 g, then 500 mg daily for 2 days) and the usual choice in pregnancy. A plain 'single dose' (also regimenNote[0]: 'a single 1 g dose for chlamydia') is the older regimen. The page never says doxycycline is first-line, so a UK reader is given the wrong first choice.
findings.suggestedFix: State that azithromycin is licensed for uncomplicated genital chlamydia but is an alternative to doxycycline in UK guidance (preferred in pregnancy); delete '(single dose)' and the 'single 1 g dose' wording.

findings.quote: Omeprazole reduces the activation of clopidogrel (pantoprazole preferred); stop two weeks before H. pylori testing
findings.explanation: Bare imperative to stop a medicine. The 2-week PPI-free interval before a breath or stool H. pylori test is correct (NICE CG184), but pausing is decided with the clinician arranging the test; people with a bleeding ulcer, Barrett oesophagus, NSAID gastroprotection or severe reflux may need other cover. Elsewhere on the page the same fact is phrased passively ('it is stopped for at least 2 weeks before testing').
findings.suggestedFix: 'PPIs are usually paused for 2 weeks before a breath or stool H. pylori test, as directed by the clinician arranging it.'

findings.quote: https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/search?q=omeprazole
findings.explanation: The source for the pharmacokinetic figures (bioavailability, peak, half-life, elimination) is an emc search-results URL, not an SmPC, so 'SmPC section 5.2' cannot be checked from it and the results change over time. The same pattern (search?q=<drug>) is used in pharmacokinetics.source for amoxicillin, losartan, lisinopril, rosuvastatin and azithromycin.
findings.suggestedFix: Link the specific SmPC page (medicines.org.uk/emc/product/...) or the BNF/DailyMed label that carries the figures.

findings.quote: Dose often needs to rise in pregnancy (increase by 25-50% and check TSH promptly), and with oestrogen, enzyme inducers
findings.explanation: Reads as an instruction to a person to increase their own dose by a stated percentage. The page says elsewhere that the dose is not changed without advice, and the site states individual doses are not given. Prescriber-directed early dose increases and TSH checks in pregnancy are real practice; the wording should describe, not instruct.
findings.suggestedFix: 'Prescribers usually increase the dose early in pregnancy and check TSH more often; anyone pregnant or planning pregnancy is advised to tell their prescriber promptly and not to change the dose themselves.'

findings.quote: a racing heartbeat or chest pain after a dose is a reason to contact a doctor
findings.explanation: Chest pain after a dose in someone with heart disease or an older person can be angina or an arrhythmia; 'a reason to contact a doctor' (and cautions[5], 'is reported to a doctor') understates the urgency. The adjacent bullets signpost NHS 111 or emergency help for other effects, so this is inconsistent.
findings.suggestedFix: Say that chest pain, or a racing or irregular heartbeat with breathlessness or faintness, needs urgent medical help (999, or NHS 111 if mild and unsure).

findings.quote: Sick-day rules: pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever
findings.explanation: Bare imperatives to stop a blood-pressure medicine. Same pattern here in sideEffects.serious[3] ('stop before or as soon as pregnancy is known') and in medications/lisinopril cautions[0] ('Sick-day rules: pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever with dehydration') and sideEffects.serious[4] ('stop as soon as pregnancy is confirmed'). The losartan warnings entry words the sick-day point better (UK information advises that it may need to be paused temporarily). Unsupervised stopping in pregnancy can leave hypertension untreated; the safe message is to speak to the prescriber promptly about a switch.
findings.suggestedFix: Describe rather than instruct: 'During a dehydrating illness prescribers may advise pausing temporarily (sick-day guidance) and restarting when eating and drinking normally; follow the prescriber's or pharmacist's advice' and 'not recommended in pregnancy; anyone pregnant or planning pregnancy should speak to their prescriber promptly about a safer alternative'.

findings.quote: Never stop long-term steroids suddenly; sick-day doubling rules.
findings.explanation: 'Sick-day doubling rules' is an unexplained instruction to change (double) the dose. Sick-day dose adjustment applies to people who have been given an individual plan (long-term steroid users, adrenal insufficiency) and needs urgent medical help if vomiting; a reader on a short course could misread it as general advice.
findings.suggestedFix: Describe it: 'People on long-term steroids are given an individual sick-day plan by their prescriber (which may include a temporary dose increase, and urgent help if they are vomiting and cannot keep tablets down); the dose is not changed without that plan.'

findings.quote: NICE: a high-intensity alternative (10-40 mg) when atorvastatin is not tolerated or contraindicated, or when lipid targets are not met
findings.explanation: On this same page 40 mg is 'reserved for specialist use', 'carries the highest risk' and is contraindicated with several predisposing factors. To my knowledge NICE's statin-intensity table lists rosuvastatin 10-20 mg (not 40 mg) as high intensity. Attributing '10-40 mg' to NICE conflicts with both.
findings.suggestedFix: Use '10-20 mg' or remove the dose range from the NICE note.

findings.quote: 20 mg and 40 mg, and longer courses
findings.explanation: otc.UK says 10 mg and 20 mg tablets are sold from pharmacies for short-term heartburn and reflux, but regulatory[0] lists only 10 mg as pharmacy and regulatory[1] puts '20 mg and 40 mg, and longer courses' under prescription. In the UK a 20 mg gastro-resistant tablet is sold as a pharmacy medicine for 14-day courses (for example Pyrocalm Control, which the page lists among UK brands), so one of the two fields is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Align them: pharmacy sale of 10 mg and 20 mg for short courses in adults; prescription for longer courses and 40 mg. Check against the NHS page and SmPC.

findings.quote: Cetirizine also exists as eye drops for itchy allergic conjunctivitis and, in some countries, as an intravenous injection for acute hives given by a healthcare professional.
findings.explanation: The eye-drop product (cetirizine ophthalmic solution) is, as far as I know, a US product with no UK licence, and the injection is also US-only. The entity contradicts itself: routeIds and dosageFormIds are oral only and regimenNote lists 'eye drops and nasal sprays of related agents', not cetirizine. On a UK-first page US-only formulations need a jurisdiction label.
findings.suggestedFix: 'In the United States cetirizine is also marketed as eye drops and as an injection...' or remove the sentence.

findings.quote: Capsules 250 and 500 mg, oral suspension, sachets; intravenous injection; usually three times daily for 5 days
findings.explanation: Frequency and duration depend on the indication, so a blanket 'usually three times daily for 5 days' is not a reliable reference summary: the omeprazole page gives 7-day PPI-based triple therapy for H. pylori (amoxicillin is given twice daily in UK regimens), other UK courses run 5 to 7 days, and the onset field says the course 'is decided by the infection'. It also reads as a dosing instruction.
findings.suggestedFix: Give strengths and forms only, or say 'frequency and duration depend on the infection and are set by the prescriber'.

findings.quote: hip fractures fall by about 40% and spine fractures by half
findings.explanation: These percentages are not in any reference cited on the page (two NHS pages and MedlinePlus). They resemble trial and meta-analysis figures for women with a previous vertebral fracture (roughly 45 to 50% for vertebral and hip fractures) but are stated unconditionally; a hip-fracture benefit was not shown in lower-risk women in primary-prevention trials, so this overstates benefit for many readers.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the percentages, or cite a source and qualify them ('in women with osteoporosis and a previous vertebral fracture').

findings.quote: Prevention of major cardiovascular events in people at high risk of a first event, and slowing the progression of atherosclerosis
findings.explanation: Marked 'licensed' for the UK with the BNF as source, but 'slowing the progression of atherosclerosis' is, to my knowledge, a US labelling indication; the UK SmPC and BNF list hypercholesterolaemia and dyslipidaemia and prevention of major cardiovascular events. The same phrase appears in usedFor[2] with no jurisdiction.
findings.suggestedFix: Move 'slowing atherosclerosis' to the US entry (MedlinePlus) or remove it from the UK-licensed note and from usedFor.

findings.quote: Otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis and tonsillitis, skin and soft-tissue infections, uncomplicated genital chlamydia and non-gonococcal urethritis, typhoid, Lyme disease (early), and prevention of Mycobacterium avium complex infection
findings.explanation: Marked 'licensed' for the UK with the BNF as source. To my recollection the UK SmPC lists sinusitis, otitis media, pharyngitis and tonsillitis, exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, mild to moderate community-acquired pneumonia, skin and soft-tissue infection and uncomplicated Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis or cervicitis; typhoid, early Lyme disease and MAC prophylaxis are guideline uses that I believe are unlicensed in the UK. Please verify against the BNF indications page.
findings.suggestedFix: Separate licensed from unlicensed (guideline-supported) uses, or remove typhoid, Lyme disease and MAC prophylaxis from the licensed list.

notes: 14 entities read in full (medications 14:28). 29 candidate issues were found; the 20 most important are listed, ordered by severity then confidence. No web access was used, so items marked low confidence (and the NICE NG138/NG238, BASHH, SmPC statements) rest on memory and should be checked against the sources. Dropped for the cap, all low: (1) individual-dose wording elsewhere that sits uneasily with the page statement 'Individual doses are not given on this page' - rosuvastatin cautions[1] 'Start at 5 mg and do not exceed 20 mg', allopurinol regimenNote 'starting at 100 mg (50 mg in kidney disease) and titrating up to 900 mg', levothyroxine 'start at 25 micrograms', lisinopril and losartan renal and older-adult starting doses; (2) allopurinol sideEffects.serious[0] says people of Han Chinese, Thai and Korean ancestry 'are screened' for HLA-B*58:01, but UK guidance says screening should be considered, not that it is routine; (3) amoxicillin: renal text 'eGFR below 30 for high doses, below 10 for standard doses' (warnings and populations.renal) may be wrong, because the SmPC reduces standard doses from CrCl 30 (low confidence); the anaphylaxis figure 'about 1 in 10,000 courses' is not in the cited references; usedFor[3] lists other drugs (nitrofurantoin, flucloxacillin, doxycycline) inside a 'used for' list and sits oddly beside the summary's 'some urinary infections'; (4) cetirizine sideEffects.common[0] 'more than 1 in 10 people' resembles US trial data, while the UK SmPC classes somnolence as common (1 in 100 to 1 in 10), so check the NHS wording; I also could not confirm the MedlinePlus ID a623043 for cetirizine (I recall a698026) without web access; (5) levothyroxine cautions[0] 'separate by 4 hours' lumps calcium, iron and antacids (4 h) with coffee (30 to 60 min) and PPIs (spacing does not remove the effect); (6) pathway chips in amoxicillin ('Growing bacteria lyse') and azithromycin ('Bacteria stop multiplying; immune clearance') link to physiology/gas-exchange, which is irrelevant; (7) sertraline: usedFor lists generalised anxiety without saying it is off-label in the UK, 'the liquid concentrate is diluted' is a US product, 'treatable and not a reason to stop' (pregnancy cautions) is a blanket continue-or-stop judgement, and the onset field (benefit at 2-4 weeks) differs from howItWorks (most feel better within a couple of weeks); (8) omeprazole and amoxicillin pregnancy and breastfeeding texts say 'safe to take', which may be stronger than the NHS 'usually safe' wording (could not verify). Several UK-first pages use US wording presented as general (see findings on rosuvastatin ciclosporin, cetirizine eye drops, rosuvastatin atherosclerosis).
